description: You are the future of engineering!
summary:
LUNA Spiculum (Lunar Unified Navigational Atlas) is an interactive web platform that helps users find and evaluate the best landing sites on the Moon. As space agencies and private companies plan new lunar missions, choosing a safe touchdown spot means balancing sunlight, temperature, terrain, and reliable communication with Earth. Our tool brings this complex analysis directly into a standard web browser.

Users can click on any specific point or select a broader zone on the Moon and choose a custom timeframe. LUNA Spiculum then simulates the motion of the Earth, Moon, and Sun over that period to calculate key environmental and engineering conditions—including surface temperature, sunlight availability, solar panel tilt, radiation levels, terrain slope, and direct radio visibility to Earth, among other key metrics.

Instead of raw numbers, the platform turns these calculations into intuitive bar charts and 2D/3D graphs, making it easy to spot trends and compare different landing windows at a glance. To ground the simulation in reality, LUNA Spiculum also features the landing coordinates of past and upcoming lunar missions. This allows anyone—from mission planners to students—to explore local conditions at historic landing sites and test whether a new target zone is truly optimal.
details:
What is LUNA Spiculum and how does it works?

LUNA Spiculum (Lunar Unified Navigational Atlas) is a browser-based simulation environment that models the coupled Earth–Moon–Sun system to evaluate lunar landing site feasibility. Instead of relying on static maps, the platform dynamically computes how lighting, thermal, topographic, radiation, and communication conditions evolve over time for any chosen location on the Moon.

1. Interactive User Workflow

  • Target Selection (Point or Gridded Zone): Users can click any single coordinate on the 3D lunar globe or define a broader target zone.
  • Custom Timeframe & Orbital Simulation: Using an interactive timeline, users select a specific timestamp or an extended observation window. The tool calculates the real-time positions and apparent disk diameters of the Sun and Earth relative to the lunar surface.
  • Mission Benchmarking: Built-in coordinates of historic and upcoming lunar missions allow users to jump directly to real landing sites, inspect their environmental profiles, and use them as a baseline to evaluate new candidate locations.

2. Physics & Engineering Calculations (Instant & Period-Averaged)

For every selected point or grid, LUNA Spiculum computes both instantaneous values and period-averaged / cumulative metrics across four core domains:

  • Topography & Horizon Geometry: Point elevation relative to the lunar datum (m), surface slope (°), sunward and earthward horizon angles, and clearance above local terrain obstacles.
  • Solar & Thermal Environment: Sun elevation and azimuth, solar incidence angle on slopes, visible solar disk percentage (accounting for local horizon obstructions and solar eclipses caused by the Earth), wait time until direct sunlight, total sunlight hours, solar irradiance (W/m²), absorbed sunlight, emitted thermal flux, net surface radiation, surface temperature (°C), and optimal solar tracker tilt angles (°).
  • Radiation Environment: Estimated radiation dose rates (µSv/h) based on galactic cosmic rays and solar wind models.
  • Earth–Moon Communications: Earth elevation and azimuth, one-way signal delay, free-space path loss, local link status, and 2.2 GHz link margin (dB) benchmarked against a 3 dB operational threshold.

3. Multi-Dimensional Visualization

To turn complex orbital and physical outputs into actionable insights, LUNA Spiculum combines three visual layers:

  • 3D Lunar Scene Overlays: Dynamic surface color scales synchronized with the simulation timeline to highlight spatial variations across zones.
  • Comparative Bar Charts: Quick visual breakdowns of key site metrics and mission benchmarks.
  • Interactive 2D & 3D Graphs: Time-series and multi-variable plots (with keyboard and cursor inspection) that reveal illumination cycles, thermal extremes, and communication windows at a glance.

What benefits does it have?

LUNA Spiculum bridges the gap between complex planetary science tools and intuitive visual exploration, offering distinct benefits for mission planners, researchers, and students alike:

  • All-in-One Decision Support: Instead of juggling separate software for orbital mechanics, terrain mapping, thermal modeling, and RF link budgets, users can evaluate lighting, surface temperature, radiation, and slope within a single unified workspace.
  • Dynamic, Terrain-Aware Realism: Unlike static lunar maps, LUNA Spiculum models how conditions actually change over time. By factoring in local horizon obstructions, surface slopes, and Earth-cast solar eclipses, it prevents overly optimistic estimates and reveals true operational windows.
  • Zero-Barrier Browser Accessibility: Built as a lightweight web application, the platform requires no expensive aerospace licenses, supercomputing hardware, or complex installation—making high-level lunar mission analysis accessible to anyone with an internet connection.
  • Instant Benchmarking Against Real Missions: Integrating coordinates from past and upcoming lunar expeditions gives users immediate real-world context. Engineers and students can see why historic sites succeeded and test candidate landing zones against proven baselines.
  • From Pinpoint Accuracy to Regional Screening: Whether analyzing a single exact touchdown coordinate or scanning a gridded region across the lunar surface, the tool scales effortlessly to highlight spatial trade-offs and optimal zones.
  • Faster Insight Through Visual Analytics: By translating dense physical formulas into synchronized 3D globe overlays, bar charts, and interactive 2D/3D plots, the platform reduces data interpretation time and makes complex spaceflight trade-offs easy to grasp at a glance.

What is the intended impact of the project?

The intended impact of LUNA Spiculum is to democratize lunar mission analysis and support humanity’s sustainable return to the Moon. As space agencies, commercial companies, and academic institutions prepare for a new era of lunar exploration, our platform makes high-level landing site evaluation accessible far beyond specialized mission control centers.

  • Accelerating Early-Stage Mission Planning: By enabling rapid, multi-parameter screening of lighting, thermal, radiation, terrain, and communication conditions, LUNA Spiculum helps mission designers and emerging lunar startups identify viable touchdown zones early—reducing planning time and helping de-risk mission concepts before committing costly engineering resources.
  • Lowering Barriers to Space Engineering: Historically, evaluating three-body orbital mechanics alongside local lunar topography required expensive proprietary software and deep domain expertise. Moving this capability into an open, intuitive web browser empowers independent researchers, university teams, and smaller aerospace organizations worldwide to participate meaningfully in lunar exploration.
  • Inspiring and Educating the Next Generation (STEM): By pairing real physics with interactive 2D/3D visualizations and historic mission landmarks, the platform transforms abstract orbital mechanics into a hands-on learning tool. Students and space enthusiasts can directly explore why past missions landed where they did and test their own hypotheses for future lunar outposts.
  • Establishing a Common Reference for Lunar Exploration: By uniting real-time simulation with past and upcoming mission datasets in one unified atlas, LUNA Spiculum fosters data-driven comparison and transparent collaboration across the global space community.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

To host our project, we used a dedicated cloud server running Linux Ubuntu. For remote access and server management over SSH, we utilized the integrated Remote-SSH extension in Visual Studio Code. The backend was developed in Python using the Flask framework, which handled user requests and delivered computation results via a JSON-based REST API. The frontend was built with JavaScript, HTML, and CSS. To create the interactive 3D model of the Moon, we used the CesiumJS library, which enabled lunar surface visualization, camera controls, space mission markers, and analysis of selected regions. To model the positions and motion of celestial bodies at any given timestamp, we used SpiceyPy, a Python wrapper for the NASA SPICE toolkit. This allowed us to compute the relative positions of the Sun, Earth, and Moon based on astronomical data and SPICE kernel files. For scientific and mathematical computations, we used the NumPy and SciPy libraries to perform numerical calculations, process data arrays, and model thermal processes in the lunar regolith. To work with lunar surface datasets, we utilized Digital Elevation Models (DEM), lunar surface imagery, and the tifffile library to process the corresponding raster data. To generate charts and visualize thermal analysis results, we used JavaScript alongside interactive web interface components. For bundling and optimizing the frontend, we used Vite, Node.js, and npm. Web serving on the cloud instance was handled by Nginx, while Gunicorn was used to run the Python backend. File transfers between our local machines and the server were performed via SCP, and updates to the deployed site were synchronized using rsync. Overall, our project combines web development, 3D graphics, backend infrastructure, numerical modeling, and real astronomical data to investigate surface conditions on the Moon.
